Publication bias We assessed publication bias using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test within the network meta-analysis. Visual inspection suggested slight asymmetry; however, Egger’s tests provided no statistically significant evidence of small-study effects for any outcome (depression: p = 0.0553, p >0.05; anxiety: p = 0.0586, p >0.05; self-esteem: p = 0.2361, p >0.05). Although minor asymmetry was noted for depression and anxiety, the potential impact of bias appears limited, supporting the overall robustness of the pooled estimates.(Detailed results are shown in additional file 4). Quality of evidence evaluation According to the CINeMA, the evidence quality was ultimately classified into two levels: low and moderate. For improving depression, comparisons of CT vs. N, CT vs. RT, and N vs. RT were rated as moderate quality data. Comparisons of CT vs. AT, RT vs. AT, and N vs. AT were influenced by study bias, imprecision, and heterogeneity, leading to a low-quality rating. For alleviating anxiety, CT vs. RT and N vs. RT were rated as moderate quality data, while CT vs. AT, RT vs. AT, N vs. AT, and CT vs. N were affected by study bias, imprecision, and heterogeneity, resulting in a low-quality rating. For enhancing self-esteem, comparisons of N vs. AT, CT vs. RT, and N vs. RT were rated as moderate quality data. However, CT vs. AT, RT vs. AT, and CT vs. N were downgraded to low quality due to study bias, imprecision, and heterogeneity. (Detailed results can be found in additional file 5,additional file 6) Discussion A total of 27 studies were included in the meta-analysis, comprising 3,059 participants. We ranked the effects of each intervention on various psychological outcomes. The results indicate that physical exercise interventions significantly improved depressive symptoms in children and adolescents. RT was found to be the most effective, followed by AT, MBE, and CT. For anxiety symptoms, CT may be effective, followed by RT, AT, and MBE. Regarding self-esteem improvement, RT demonstrated the best results, followed by AT, MBE, and CT. Exercise has been demonstrated to exert a positive effect in ameliorating mental health issues such as depression, anxiety, and self-esteem among children and adolescents [ 19 , 56 , 57 ]. Among youth, aerobic training, resistance training, combined aerobic-resistance training, and mind-body exercise are the modalities most frequently implemented as intervention. Aerobic training is a principal component of school physical education and has been shown to induce neurogenesis, thereby promoting learning, memory, and emotion regulation in children and adolescents and mitigating depressive symptoms [ 58 ]. Resistance training implemented as part of multicomponent exercise regimens, school physical education curricula, and after-school fitness programs [ 59 , 60 ]has garnered increasing attention. Through muscle-brain crosstalk involving the release of myokines and related factors, RT modulates immune function [ 61 ], attenuates stress dysregulation associated with adverse psychological states [ 62 ], and reduces cardiovascular disease risk [ 63 ]. Combined aerobic and resistance exercise encompasses diverse, engaging formats that achieve high participation among children and adolescents. Such programs are associated with improved social functioning, reductions in body weight among youth with obesity, enhanced metabolic health [ 64 ], and attenuation of inflammatory status [ 65 ]. Mind-body exercise comprises traditional practices that integrate physical activity with focused attention to promote holistic health through coordinated movements, controlled breathing, and enhanced mental concentration. By modulating the release of neurotransmitters (e.g., endorphins and dopamine), MBE can elevate positive affect [ 20 , 66 ]and, in parallel, induce favorable changes in the functional organization of the cerebral cortex, thereby contributing to improved mental health. Despite the significant impact of diverse exercise interventions on the mental health of children and adolescents, their modality-specific benefits warrant further investigation to strengthen the empirical basis for clinical implementation. The SUCRA results of this study indicate that RT demonstrates a significantly greater advantage in improving depressive symptoms, consistent with previous findings [ 67 , 68 ]. The mechanism of action of RT may be attributed to short-term, high-intensity stimulation that enhances the expression of neurotrophic factors [ 69 ], reduces inflammatory responses [ 70 ], and strengthens synaptic connections between neurons [ 71 ], ultimately improving depressive symptoms. Furthermore, RT can effectively enhance muscle performance by increasing muscle strength, bone density, and the recruitment of motor neurons, thereby improving the overall coordination between muscles and nerves [ 72 ].From a psychological perspective, RT helps children experience a tangible sense of strength gains [ 73 ], which enhances their body image affirmation and self-esteem, thereby improving depression [, 75 ]. Despite numerous studies investigating the optimal exercise modality for alleviating depression, there remains some controversy. For example, studies by Li [ 76 ] and Wang [ 77 ] suggest that AT has a more significant effect on depression improvement, while Yu et al. [ 78 ] found that CT yields the best results. In contrast, high-intensity interval training was deemed the most effective for treating depression in university students [ 79 ]. These discrepancies may be attributed to differences in the study populations and the heterogeneity of the included literature.In this study, we selected children and adolescents aged 7 to 18 years as participants. In contrast to university student populations, children and adolescents exhibit significant physiological developmental differences. Adolescents at this stage are more sensitive to hormones, possess greater neuroplasticity, and exhibit faster improvements in motor skill learning and neuromuscular coordination. Additionally, adolescents’ cognitive abilities are still developing and are in a critical period for habit formation. During this period, adolescents show more positive adherence to RT and greater psychological perception compared to university students, which leads to higher exercise completion rates and enhances the effects of RT. For alleviating anxiety, the cumulative ranking probability indicates that CT may be advantageous, yielding greater effects than AT or RT alone. Prior studies indicate that, compared with AT alone, CT yields greater improvements in functional exercise capacity and respiratory outcomes among adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis [ 80 ]. CT has also been shown to effectively control pediatric obesity and to reduce cardiovascular risk [ 81 ]and body mass index [ 82 ]. However, evidence regarding its effects on anxiety symptoms in children and adolescents remains limited. The underlying mechanism may be attributed to the following: First, exercise-induced myokine interleukin-6 upregulates anti-inflammatory mediators interleukin-1 receptor antagonist and interleukin-10 production while concurrently suppressing TNF-α. Functioning as an acute anti-inflammatory signal, this IL-6 mediated pathway has been documented after both aerobic and resistance exercise; when combined in a CT regimen, the effects may be additive, thereby enhancing the overall efficacy of the intervention [ 83 ]. This anti-inflammatory cascade can, in turn, attenuate anxiety-related peripheral inflammation and metabolic stress and is accompanied by a broader myokine response [ 84 ]. Second, exercise can improve neural function through different signaling pathways. Aerobic and resistance modalities activate neuroplasticity through distinct signaling pathways [ 85 ], exert synergistic neurotrophic effects and potentiate immunoregulatory responses [ 86 ], while concurrently improving cardiorespiratory function and augmenting muscular strength [ 87 ]. Third, exercise can enhance the body’s tolerance to anxiety. AT and RT target partially distinct domains in the treatment of anxiety: AT preferentially mitigates general psychological distress and state anxiety, whereas RT more robustly improves disorder-specific symptoms, reduces anxiety sensitivity, and enhances distress tolerance as well as tolerance of uncertainty (i.e., lowers intolerance of uncertainty) [ 88 ]. Consequently, CT may integrate these complementary effects to yield broader and more effective anxiolytic benefits. Fourth, From the perspective of children and adolescents, the diversified mix of activities in CT offers a more game-like and engaging experience, effectively increasing exercise frequency and willingness to participate, enhancing social interaction, and fostering intrinsic motivation for autonomous participation in physical training. In the pairwise meta-analysis, we did not observe a statistically significant reduction in anxiety symptoms among children and adolescents (MD=−0.12, p <0.001, 95%CI[−0.32,0.09], I 2 = 73.5%). Several factors may have attenuated observable effects. First, most trials were modest in size, limiting statistical power and increasing the risk of type II error. Second, anxiety outcomes were assessed using different instruments with varying sensitivity to change, which may dilute pooled effects. Third, incomplete reporting of allocation concealment and blinding in some studies may introduce bias, and heterogeneity in intervention delivery (modality, intensity, supervision) further complicates inference. Future trials should predefine moderator analyses (e.g., sex, age band, baseline severity, and standardized dose parameters), adopt harmonized outcome measures, and ensure adequate sample sizes to more precisely delineate whether particular modalities or doses yield clinically meaningful anxiolytic effects. This study found that exercise significantly improves the self-esteem of children and adolescents, which is consistent with previous research [ 89 ]. Putative mechanisms may include the following: exercise elevates circulating BDNF in adolescents, thereby enhancing plasticity in the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex [ 90 ], modulating the function of neural circuits involved in affective processing and strengthening positive self-appraisal. Exercise may also upregulate the endocannabinoid(eCB) system [ 91 ], which can diminish negative affect and promote feelings of pleasure. In addition, when children and adolescents experience symptoms of depression and anxiety, not only do they reduce social interactions with peers, but they also experience a decline in self-esteem and self-efficacy, thereby increasing the risks of suicide, criminal behavior, and other adverse outcomes [ 92 ]. Children with low self-esteem typically exhibit strong social avoidance behaviors and low willingness to engage in physical activity. They tend to avoid peer interactions or participation in group activities, which affects their social competence and the development of close relationships. Prolonged states of low self-esteem can have profound impacts on children’s academic performance, mental health, and overall quality of life, potentially laying the foundation for more severe psychological issues, such as depression, in the future.According to the SUCRA results, RT has the most significant effect in enhancing self-esteem. In line with prior research, depression has been shown to have a neurobiological link to self-esteem [ 93 ], and after depression treatment, positive self-cognition is also improved [ 94 ]. Therefore, our findings are highly credible, suggesting that RT has a dual effect in treating depression and enhancing self-cognition.From a psychological perspective, compared to other types of exercise, RT in children and adolescents is more structured, typically accompanied by higher levels of supervision and control. This structured intervention effectively reduces children’s and adolescents’ focus on negative emotions, while simultaneously enhancing their sense of social belonging, further improving their self-esteem and sports performance [ 21 ]. Based on our findings, in addition to strengthening the education on mental health awareness and increasing the participation in physical activities, the mediating role of social support should be fully leveraged [ 25 ]. Appropriate resistance training should be incorporated into school physical education curricula and personalised exercise prescriptions. Common forms of MBE include yoga, Tai Chi, Qigong, and Baduanjin. These practices emphasize the coordinated interplay of physical postures, breath regulation, and focused attention to enhance physical fitness, psychological well-being, and emotional balance. In the present analysis, however, mind-body exercise operationalized as yoga and Tai Chi did not yield statistically significant improvements in mental health outcomes among children and adolescents. Synthesizing prior meta-analytic evidence, the mental-health benefits of MBE remain uncertain [ 95 – 98 ]. Several factors may account for this uncertainty. First, MBE is generally of low-to-moderate intensity and acts primarily through autonomic and respiratory regulation, whereas reward-system sensitivity closely linked to adolescent anxiety and depression and molecular pathways such as BDNF and eCB system are strongly intensity dependent. Moderate-to-vigorous aerobic training most consistently elicits eCB-mediated hedonic/anxiolytic responses [ 99 ], and higher-intensity or interval protocol more likely to upregulate BDNF [ 69 ]. Consequently, the effects of MBE may be comparatively limited. Second, pediatric health guidelines recommend ≥ 60 min of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily and vigorous-intensity activity on ≥ 3 days per week to enhance muscular strength [ 74 , 75 ], thresholds that many school-based yoga or Tai Chi classes fail to meet in either intensity or volume. Third, the included studies reported higher attrition in MBE than in other modalities, potentially reflecting insufficient dynamic stimulation, poor alignment with participants’ interests or needs, and limited short-term positive reinforcement, all of which may reduce adherence and engagement [ 100 ]. In addition, several trials had small sample sizes and were conducted in general school populations rather than clinical cohorts, making significant improvements more difficult to detect [ 101 ]. Cultural variability in the acceptability of traditional MBE may further hinder dissemination and uptake, and MBE’s benefits may accrue over longer time frames, such that short-duration interventions underestimate its effects [ 102 ]. Therefore, future research should endeavour to expand sample sizes, focus on longer-term intervention cycles, and optimise exercise guidance programmes to enhance the scientific rigour, practicality, and adherence of mind-body exercise. This will enable a more comprehensive assessment of its potential benefits for the mental health of children and adolescents. Limitation However, this study has several limitations. First, restricting inclusion to English-language publications may have introduced selection bias and contributed to publication bias. Second, few studies adequately reported allocation concealment and blinding, increasing the risk of selection/performance bias and weakening internal validity. Third, the absence of individual participant data constrained analyses to study-level aggregates, precluding consistent adjustment for key confounders (e.g., intervention duration, intensity, modality, sex, age, overall dose) and likely contributing to the observed heterogeneity. Fourth, intervention cycles, intensities, and session durations lacked standardized dosing and control, and notable imbalances in sample size across studies may have biased pooled estimates and lowered the certainty of evidence; greater methodological harmonization is warranted. Fifth, control conditions varied in content and intensity, potentially introducing bias and reducing comparability. Sixth, the inclusion of older trials that predate contemporary diagnostic criteria and modern exercise prescriptions may limit comparability with current practice. Seventh, this review was limited to unimodal exercise interventions and did not evaluate multimodal programs, which may constrain ecological validity and real-world applicability. Conclusion Exercise appears effective for reducing depressive symptoms and enhancing self-esteem in children and adolescents, and may also confer benefits for anxiety. Effects vary by modality: resistance training shows an advantage for improving depression and self-esteem, whereas combined aerobic-resistance programs may help alleviate anxiety. However, given the small number of included studies, their overall moderate methodological quality, and indications of publication bias and between-study heterogeneity, these conclusions should be interpreted cautiously and require further verification. Future research should stratify and/or meta-regress by sex, age, and exercise dose (e.g., frequency, intensity, duration, and modality) to strengthen the evidence base and inform more effective strategies to prevent or reduce depression, anxiety, and low self-esteem in youth.
